sentences: We are at a Paris crossroads where the wet paving stones shine.
A couple sharing one umbrella walks toward us.
The canvas is more than 2.
7 metres wide and the figures are close to life-size, so we seem to stand on the street ourselves.
This is today's Place de Dublin, minutes from the Gare Saint-Lazare.
When Gustave Caillebotte was a boy it was a tangle of narrow, crooked streets, until Baron Haussmann's rebuilding laid out wide new avenues.
His family home stood nearby.
Look at the building in the distance, pointed like the prow of a ship.
New buildings of equal height and identical windows stretch along each boulevard.
This orderly, austere view is the new face of Haussmann's Paris.
On the left a carriage waits, and passers-by with umbrellas cross the rainy square.
Each goes his own way, and no one looks at anyone else.
In the widened city, the distance between people seems to have widened too.
Now look down at the paving stones at your feet.
Each square stone is wet with rain and holds a faint shine.
The foreground is crisp while the distance blurs, much as it would through a camera lens.
Look at the green lamppost in the middle.
It divides the scene exactly in half.
On the left lies the open square, on the right the figures right in front of us, so far and near sit side by side.
The couple on the right walk together under one umbrella, gazing at something outside the picture.
With his top hat and her fine coat, the two are well-dressed citizens of the new city, at ease on its boulevard.
The man on the far right is cropped by the edge of the canvas.
We see neither his whole body nor his whole umbrella, as if a photograph had been trimmed.
The street seems to carry on beyond the frame.
Caillebotte built this street with a precise two-point perspective.
A popular theory holds that he traced his preparatory sketches from photographs.
A 2015 Art Institute report suggests he more likely used an optical drawing aid called a camera lucida.
The picture made its debut at the third Impressionist exhibition in April 1877, where one critic called it the masterpiece of the show.
Caillebotte largely organised the exhibitions from then on.
The Art Institute of Chicago bought it in 1964.
Step back and take in the whole canvas.
Life-size figures stroll toward us, and we share the same pavement.
What do you imagine the couple are looking at, just beyond the edge of the picture?
